EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Unseasonably mild air moved into the region ahead of a strong low pressure system. These conditions, on top of a fairly dry February across western South Dakota allowed a fire to develop northeast of the community of Green Grass and spread rapidly southeast. 991 acres of mostly prairie and pasture were burned in the fire, with a portion of Highway 63 closed due to smoke and the threat of the fire crossing the Highway. ||Winds picked up dramatically with the passage of the low pressure system, with a peak wind gust of 81 mph recorded at the Pierre Regional Airport ASOS. The South Dakota Department of Transportation (SDDOT) Road Weather Information System (RWIS) 1 mile west northwest of Summit recorded a wind gust as high as 79 mph, while the SDDOT RWIS 3 miles southeast of Reliance recorded a peak wind of 77 mph. Another 23 weather stations would record a peak wind in excess of 70 mph. ||These high winds were responsible for at least one semi being blown off Interstate 29 near Summit, forcing a closure of the southbound lane.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS at the Pierre Regional Airport recorded a peak wind gust of 81 mph, while a nearby mesonet station recorded a wind gust to 75 mph. Additionally, the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonets 1 mile east northeast of Harrold and 9 miles east southeast of Rosseau recorded gusts of 71 and 70 mph respectively. 2 additional weather stations would go on to record peak wind gusts in excess of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful, but rather moisture starved low pressure system moved across the Northern Plains March 12-13. Widespread high winds raced across the region late on the 12th and into the early overnight of the 13th with gusts ranging from 58 to 78 mph behind a strong cold front. With little to no snow on the ground, there were no significant reductions in visibility.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 52 mph at times, with gusts as high as 74 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Wolsey.

A system brought locally heavy snow and strong winds ranging from 45 to 55 mph to northeast South Dakota. Due to deteriorating conditions on March 14th, Interstate 29 north of Watertown and several highways across the northeast and north central parts of the state were closed. The COOP observer 1 mile southwest of Clear Lake recorded 8 inches of snow, while the CoCoRaHS observer in La Bolt measured a total of 6.2 inches.||Falling snow ended before the winds increased, resulting in only intermittent, short-lived blizzard conditions.  The Andover COOP and a CoCoRaHS observer 6 miles southwest of Gary reported near-blizzard conditions at the time of their observations.

From March 15 through the early hours of March 16, a low-pressure system rapidly intensified over the Central Plains, generating a powerful wind field with gusts reaching 45 to 65 mph. Although limited antecedent snow cover ���maxing out at 1 to 2 inches in parts of the James River Valley���initially delayed widespread blowing snow, conditions deteriorated as precipitation intensified early on the 15th. In northwest Iowa, the storm began with several hours of freezing rain, resulting in ice accumulations of one-tenth to one-third of an inch. Additionally, plummeting temperatures created hazardous wind chills ranging from 15 below to 30 below zero.||Transportation was severely disrupted, leading to the closure of the Sioux Falls Regional Airport and most state and federal highways north of Interstate 90; travel was discouraged in nearly all other areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northerly winds gusted as high as 55 mph 8 miles north of Yankton, 53 mph near Gayville, and 48 mph at Yankton. During and after a period of snowfall which totaled 3.0 at Yankton, visibility was reduced to one-quarter mile or less at times with blowing snow.

At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

Snowfall rapidly dropped in intensity by the late morning of April 4th. A grand total of 14 inches was recorded near Artas and 3 miles southwest of Greenway, while the EM of Dewey County estimated 12 inches of snow for Timber Lake, with 12 inches also estimated in Hecla (Brown County). ||Corson and Dewey County Sheriff and Emergency Management issued a No Travel Advised for the counties at 1045 am. Because of mild temperatures in March and early April, most roads stayed ice free during this system.

Showers and weak thunderstorms generated high winds across portions of central and north central South Dakota from the afternoon of April 22nd into the early morning hours of April 23rd. A peak wind gust of 71 mph was recorded at the Sand Lake RAWS 13 miles east northeast of Eureka, and at the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 5 miles north of Reliance. Winds were strong enough 5 miles east of Pollock to flatten a 10 by 10 outbuilding and gazebo, and power poles were snapped 6 miles north northeast of Eureka, with a loss of power to 615 customers. Power outages were also reported in Walworth county to 108 customers. The lightning overnight sparked a 30 acre fire near the town of Barnard in Brown county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms brought little rainfall, with hail to the size of nickels and wind gusts around 50 mph. Lightning also started fires nearby.

At late afternoon, considerable moisture focused near a strong warm front from low pressure across northeastern Nebraska through northwest Iowa. Climatologically significant mid-level lapse rates produced a strong capping inversion which gradually weakened north of the warm front. Storms initiated with effective deep-layer shear from 40 to 50 knots and quickly became severe hail producers north of the warm front across southeast South Dakota into southwest Minnesota during the late afternoon, with additional storms developing in proximity to the surface wave across northwest Iowa. One of these latter storms produced two weak tornadoes across northwest Iowa.

Containment and mop up was achieved by 6:59 CST.

Two cold fronts associated with an elongated surface low pressure system swept across southeast South Dakota during the evening of February 17 and into the morning of February 18. Periods of sustained winds from 40 to 50 mph with gusts as high as 66 mph were reported across the area. The strongest winds were along and west of the James River Valley. Light snow developed along the Highway 14 corridor where a few areas picked up a half-inch up to two inches of accumulation. Related reductions in visibility were brief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were between 40 and 42 mph at times at a South Dakota Mesonet station 6 miles south of Madison.

Light snow developed along the Highway 14 corridor where a few areas picked up a half-inch up to two inches of accumulation. Related reductions in visibility were brief.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds were briefly between 40 and 41 mph at a South Dakota Road Weather Information System site near Alexandria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of snow set up across northeast South Dakota on the morning of February 28th. 8.3 inches of fluffy light snow was measured 4 miles north of Bristol, with 6.1 inches in Doland. Observers in Chelsea, Columbia, Garden City and 2 miles north of the Hamlin Education Center all submitted 6 inches of total snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP observer in Columbia measured 6 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact short-wave within northwest flow aloft moved across the Northern Plains late February 27 into February 28. Mid-level frontogenesis and sufficient moisture resulted in a narrow band of light to moderate snow mainly along and north of a De Smet, SD to Windom, MN line. These areas received 1-5 inches of snow. Winds were light during the snowfall, limiting blowing and drifting.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totaled 4.7 inches 6.5 miles north-northwest of Brookings, 4.0 inches 2.2 miles south-southeast of Astoria and 1.6 miles south of Brookings, and 3.8 inches in Aurora.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado was observed in an open field around 2 miles west of Davis. The tornado was estimated to touch down north of U.S. Highway 18 east of 458th Avenue and tracked northeast for less than a minute before it lifted just west of 459th Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 20 yards based on video evidence.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.

Very warm temperatures led to a well-mixed lower atmosphere. Weak winds and a weakly convergence boundary in the presence of marginal moisture led to the development of high-based convection, which featured a widely viewed landspout that drifted west-southwest from Minnesota into South Dakota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This landspout formed about 2 miles northwest of Hills in Rock County and entered Minnehaha County about 4 miles west-northwest of Hills.  The tornado continued to the west-southwest for a little less than a mile before dissipating just northeast of the intersection of 266th Street and 487th Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating in either Rock County or Minnehaha County, giving the tornado a rating of EFU in both counties. The average path width was estimated at 40 yards based on video and photo evidence.

Isolated strong storms produced high winds, hail and flooding in portions of northeast South Dakota. Hail to the size of quarters was recorded 6 miles southeast of the town of Roscoe and near the town of Leola. Additionally, winds were estimated at 60 mph 5 miles north northeast of Leola, with a 59 mph peak wind recorded on the Sand Lake RAWS. The primary impact of these storms was the heavy rainfall around the Leola area. The SDSU mesonet station on the east side of Leola recorded 5.48 inches of moisture with this system. Flooding in the town of Leola impacted many residents with street and basement flooding. 6 to 12 inches of water was observed covering portions of Highway 10 just west of town and heavy equipment was required to move water and debris. Highway 45 south of town was also impassible due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A second round of high winds and snow showers created hazardous travel conditions across northeast South Dakota. Although snow accumulations were minor, totaling only 2 inches or less, the light snow led to slick roads and intermittent near-blizzard conditions. These conditions resulted in several accidents, including a vehicle rollover on Interstate 90 near Vivian and a jackknifed semi-trailer on Highway 12 west of Aberdeen. The highest wind gust of 63 mph was recorded by South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet stations near Roscoe and Bowdle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A two vehicle accident limited travel for a portion of Highway 212 5 miles east of Clark. The South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station 7 miles east of Clark reported a peak wind gust of 31 mph at 2pm with snow showers.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak weather system combined with an arctic blast to bring high winds and light snow to the region on the morning of January 21. The Pierre Regional Airport ASOS measured the strongest wind gust at 76 mph. Matching 75 mph gusts were recorded by a personal weather station north of Pierre and the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station southeast of Reliance. While the Watertown COOP recorded 2.4 inches of snow, most other locations received an inch or less. The combination of wind and snow prompted No Travel Advised notices for Walworth, Hand, Faulk, Spink, Roberts, and Hamlin counties. Slick roads and intermittent low visibility resulted in a number of slide-ins across Roberts county.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Day county Sheriff issued No Travel Advised for Day county with the visibility near zero at times thanks to the combination of snow showers and strong winds. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak weather system combined with an arctic blast to bring high winds and light snow to the region on the morning of January 21. The Pierre Regional Airport ASOS measured the strongest wind gust at 76 mph. Matching 75 mph gusts were recorded by a personal weather station north of Pierre and the South Dakota Department of Transportation mesonet station southeast of Reliance. While the Watertown COOP recorded 2.4 inches of snow, most other locations received an inch or less. The combination of wind and snow prompted No Travel Advised notices for Walworth, Hand, Faulk, Spink, Roberts, and Hamlin counties. Slick roads and intermittent low visibility resulted in a number of slide-ins across Roberts county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The South Dakota Highway Patrol warned of icy roads and low visibility on Interstate 29, which led to a number of vehicle slide-ins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic high pressure moving into the area resulted in extreme cold and dangerous wind chills.
